The Leatherfin lumpsucker Eumicrotremus derjugini exhibits a life history closely tied to the extreme cold of its Arctic and subarctic habitats. Embryonic development proceeds at a remarkably slow pace, with the chorion rupture of the fertilised ovum occurring after approximately 70 days [ab = approximately 70 days] under ambient conditions of 0.2 °C [T = 0.2 °C]. This protracted hatching age is a direct consequence of the low metabolic rates sustained in near-freezing waters. Upon emergence, the yolk-sac larva is exceptionally small, with an initial wet weight at birth of just 0.001 grams [Wwb = 0.001 grams]. This minute size, derived from an egg diameter of only 1.2 millimeters, imposes a severe challenge for the lecithotrophic larva, which must progress rapidly through the yolk absorption stage to begin exogenous feeding before its limited reserves are exhausted. The transition to the exotrophic phase represents a critical bottleneck in the early life history of this species.

Growth during the postflexion larva and pelagic larval phase is characteristically slow, yet in the context of a stable, cold environment, this pace yields a predictable trajectory toward sexual maturity. Field surveys indicate that females attain the critical threshold for puberty at a total length of 4.3 cm [Lp = 4.3 cm]. At this size, the corresponding wet weight at puberty is approximately 1.74 grams [Wwp = approximately 1.74 grams], a value derived from the observed length-weight relationship for the species. The progression to this stage is not rapid; the time since birth at puberty is one year (one year since birth) [tp = one year since birth], a duration again measured at 0.2 °C [T = 0.2 °C]. This relatively slow somatic development is consistent with the pattern seen in other cyclopterids inhabiting high-latitude ecosystems, where the brief seasonal productivity window constrains the accumulation of body mass.

As individuals continue to grow past puberty, they eventually approach their ultimate size, which represents the maximum recorded body mass for the species. The ultimate total length for Eumicrotremus derjugini has been measured at 11.3 cm [Li = 11.3 cm], a modest size typical of the genus. Correspondingly, the ultimate wet weight of the Leatherfin lumpsucker is 32.4 grams [Wwi = 32.4 grams], representing the asymptotic mass attained after the period of most rapid mass gain has concluded. This weight is achieved only after several years of growth under the thermal regime of 0.2 °C [T = 0.2 °C]. The substantial increase in body mass from the sub-adult stage to the adult stage, from 1.74 grams to 32.4 grams, illustrates a roughly 18-fold gain in body mass, which supports the higher fecundity and competitive ability required for successful reproduction in a resource-limited environment.

Reproductive output in this species is constrained by both body size and the extreme cold, which lengthens inter-spawning intervals. A sexually mature female, having undergone gonad maturation, will typically produce a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year] during the brief summer period. Within each spawning event, fecundity is moderate, with gravid individuals yielding approximately 5.5 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 5.5 eggs per clutch]. This combination of a low annual frequency and a modest clutch size results in a very limited total annual reproductive output, a life-history trade-off that is common among small-bodied, cold-water teleosts. The reliance on a single annual spawning event underscores the physiological constraint imposed by the prolonged period of yolk deposition and oocyte development at low temperatures, ensuring that each batch of eggs receives sufficient yolk reserves for successful embryogenesis.

Although detailed demographic records are sparse for this species, available data on longevity suggest a compressed life cycle typical of small, cold-adapted fishes. The maximum lifespan of the Leatherfin lumpsucker in the wild is estimated at 3 years [am = 3 years], a value recorded at 0.2 °C [T = 0.2 °C]. This relatively brief existence means that most individuals likely participate in only two or three reproductive seasons before natural mortality claims them. The period from hatching to the first spawning event, which occurs shortly after the attainment of sexual maturity, is thus a critical window for population recruitment. The combination of a 70-day incubation period and a 365-day interval between birth and puberty—slow developmental rates observed across all life stages—demonstrates how the stenothermal physiology of this species has evolved to match the persistent cold of its environment.
